# CHECKS

1. Costume recognisability — for each costumed character, name any garment that breaks this: Every garment is one that costume is known for, named with the word that names it there. A garment that only hints at the theme does not count, and neither does one borrowed from a different costume or named with a word belonging to one.
2. Drawability — name any garment whose written form invites the wrong shape: headwear described by how it is knotted or fastened rather than by what it is, a garment described only by its trim or fastening, or any wording an illustrator could read as a different garment.
3. Colour distinction — name any two characters whose largest garment shares a dominant colour. Name any colour that breaks this: Every colour is one of these words, alone: red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, brown, black, white, grey. No shade name, no modifier (dark, light, pale) and no compound.
4. Slot conflicts — name any character whose outfit breaks this: One state per garment slot: never two garments in one slot that exclude each other, and a slot the character does not wear is omitted, never written out as empty.
5. Face — name any garment that breaks this: No garment covers the face or the eyes, or shadows them with a brim: no mask, visor, veil, helmet, crown or low brim. Glasses are identity, not a garment: a character whose outfit lists glasses keeps them, and every rewrite of that outfit still lists them.
6. Completeness — name any character whose outfit is missing a top, a bottom or footwear. An outfit that replaces the legs (a tail, a fin, a fused lower body) needs no bottom or footwear; it breaks this: A costume that replaces the legs (a tail, a fin) is one tail from the waist down, written as replacing the legs. Never a skirt over legs, and no feet, bare feet or footwear. Rewrite such an outfit as one tail from the waist down replacing the legs. A `nightwear` outfit needs a top and a bottom but no footwear: slippers, socks or bare feet are all complete.
7. Style world — only when a world is named below. Name any character wearing nothing from that world, and any character whose whole outfit has been replaced by it rather than accented.
8. Sex — name any character whose outfit breaks this: A male character wears garments made for boys or men, a female character garments made for girls or women. When a costume has a male and a female form, each character wears the form matching theirs. Replace the garment with that character's form of it, never by removing the slot.
9. Coverage — name any character listed under `Characters:` whom a page costumes or transforms (a tail, wings, an animal form, a disguise) and whose wardrobe has no category covering that appearance. Add the missing entry under the heading `## <CharacterName> / costumed:<costume>` with the full outfit describing the transformed or costumed appearance. Also name any character a page puts in bed, or into pyjamas for a bedtime routine at night (an adult in bed included, an adult who only sits at a bedside excluded), whose wardrobe has no `nightwear` entry. Add it under the heading `## <CharacterName> / nightwear` with the full pyjama outfit. Nightwear is two-piece pyjamas: a top covering the torso from shoulders to waist (long or short sleeve) and pyjama bottoms (long or shorts). Slippers or socks may be worn, or bare feet. Never a vest or singlet, a bare chest or midriff, or a one-piece or nightdress. Animals, creatures and other figures of the plan have no wardrobe here; never add one.
10. Child coverage — name any child whose outfit breaks this: A child's swimwear, costume or nightwear always has a covering top: a long-sleeve or short-sleeve `swim shirt` (rash-guard) over the whole torso, shoulders to waist (nightwear: the pyjama top the nightwear rule defines). Never a `bikini`, a bare chest, a bare midriff, or a one-piece (a skirt or tail below it leaves the torso reading bare). A child's `nightwear` outfit breaks it too when it breaks this: Nightwear is two-piece pyjamas: a top covering the torso from shoulders to waist (long or short sleeve) and pyjama bottoms (long or shorts). Slippers or socks may be worn, or bare feet. Never a vest or singlet, a bare chest or midriff, or a one-piece or nightdress.
11. Garment variety — name any two characters who break this: Two characters never wear the same set of garments recoloured, neither the whole outfit nor what is left once a page takes an outer layer off. A child's covering top and a leg-replacing tail are never the garment given up: vary colour, sleeve length, neckline and trim around them. Rewrite one with different garment types and silhouette; the story world decides the wardrobe.
12. Plot garments — name any garment the page plan uses as an object (held, lent, wrapped, lost) that no outfit names, or that the outfit names as a different garment. Rewrite the outfit of the character who wears it first (the one the plan first gives it to, when no one wears it) so it wears that garment, described as worn — never when, where or to whom it is lent or taken off. A garment belongs to ONE outfit: that of the character who wears it first. When the plan hands it to another character — to hold, wrap, wear or keep — the plan line and that page's `wornItems` row carry the handoff; the receiver's outfit never names it. No two outfits name the same garment. A garment another character's outfit already names is never added to a second outfit, whoever the plan hands it to. Name any garment two outfits both name, and rewrite the outfit of the character who does not wear it first without it.
13. Appearance only — An outfit `description` is appearance only: garments, colours, materials, fastenings. No page numbers, no events, no other character or creature, no carried item or what a pocket holds. A garment a page takes off stays in the outfit as worn; the `wornItems` row of that page records it off, never the outfit. Name any outfit that carries more, and rewrite it as the appearance alone.
14. Props — A garment is clothing a person wears: coat, scarf, hat, cloak, boots. A blanket, towel, sheet, tablecloth, bag, umbrella, toy, tool or any other object that is carried, held, spread out, shared or wrapped around someone for a page is a story prop, never a garment: no outfit names it, however the plan uses it. The plan line and the Visual Bible carry a prop. Name any outfit that lists a prop, and rewrite it without it.

Fixing check 1 outranks fixing check 3: a character in the right costume sharing a colour with someone else is better than a distinct colour on a garment that does not read as the costume. Two characters of different age or sex may wear the same headwear.

A rewrite must not create a fault of its own. Before writing a corrected outfit, check it against every other character's outfit — including the ones you are leaving alone — and against the outfit you are replacing. Swapping two colours between characters leaves them as hard to tell apart as before.



# OUTPUT FORMAT

Both blocks, in this order, nothing before or after.

---ANALYSIS---
<your answer to every check, by number>

---CLOTHING---
## <CharacterName> / <category>
<corrected full outfit — every slot the character wears, each with colour and material, as one self-contained description>
GARMENTS: <a JSON array of {"slot", "name", "colour"} rows for exactly the garments that outfit names>

Every fault a check names must produce a corrected or added entry below — naming a fault and answering NONE leaves it in the book.

`garments` lists every garment `description` names, one row each: `slot` is where on the body it is worn, exactly one of `headwear`, `top`, `bottom`, `footwear`, `belt/waist`, `outer layer`, `accessories`; `name` is the garment's noun phrase as `description` words it, without its colour ("hooded anorak", "canvas trainers"); `colour` is its main colour, one of red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, brown, black, white, grey and nothing else, or omitted when the garment has no single main colour. A row for every garment `description` names, and none for anything it does not.

Under a heading write the outfit, then its GARMENTS line, and nothing else: no reasoning, no commentary, no correction of what you just wrote. Rework it before you write it. One heading per character and category.

Include a character and category only if you rewrote or added it. Use the character's real name and the category exactly as it appears above. When nothing needs rewriting, still output the analysis, then:

---CLOTHING---

---ANALYSIS---
1. Costume recognisability — Lily / standard: no issue. Lily / costumed (mermaid): the outfit has a long-sleeve purple swim shirt (rash-guard) and a single flowing orange silk scarf tied at the waist as a mermaid tail that replaces the legs. A "scarf tied at the waist as a mermaid tail" is not a garment a mermaid costume is known for; it is an improvised pretend tail made from a scarf. This breaks the check. The costume needs a proper mermaid tail garment.
2. Drawability — Lily / costumed: "a single flowing orange silk scarf tied at the waist as a mermaid tail that replaces the legs from the waist down, with a loose fan-shaped fin of fabric at the end" is described by how it is knotted and fastened rather than by what it is. An illustrator could read this as a scarf wrapped around the waist rather than a tail garment. This breaks the check.
3. Colour distinction — Lily / standard: blue top. No other character, so no clash. Colours used: blue, green, brown, purple, orange, yellow — all are from the allowed list. No issue.
4. Slot conflicts — Lily / costumed: "a single flowing orange silk scarf tied at the waist as a mermaid tail that replaces the legs from the waist down" — the tail replaces the legs, which is correct; no bottom or footwear listed. No conflict. Lily / nightwear: bare feet listed as footwear. "Bare feet" is writing out a slot as empty. This breaks the check.
5. Face — No garment covers the face or eyes or shadows them with a brim. No issue.
6. Completeness — Lily / costumed: the mermaid tail replaces the legs, but it is described as a scarf tied at the waist, not as one tail from the waist down. The outfit is missing a proper tail garment and instead uses a scarf that reads as a skirt over legs. This breaks the check. Lily / nightwear: has top and bottom; bare feet is complete per the rule (nightwear needs top and bottom, no footwear required; bare feet is acceptable but the slot being written as empty is a slot conflict, not a completeness issue). No completeness issue for nightwear beyond slot.
7. Style world — No named world with specific clothing requirements in the instructions. No issue.
8. Sex — Lily is female. All garments are for girls/women. No issue.
9. Coverage — Lily appears in a mermaid costume on pages 1, 2, 5, 6. The wardrobe has a costumed entry. Lily lies in bed on page 4. The wardrobe has a nightwear entry. No missing entry. No issue.
10. Child coverage — Lily / costumed: the swim shirt is long-sleeve and covers the torso from shoulders to waist. No bikini, bare chest, bare midriff, or one-piece. The tail replaces legs. Correct. Lily / nightwear: short-sleeve yellow cotton pyjama top covering torso, matching bottoms. No vest, singlet, bare chest, bare midriff, one-piece or nightdress. Correct.
11. Garment variety — Only one character, Lily. Different outfits across categories. No issue.
12. Plot garments — The shell bracelet is a key plot object, worn by Mia (not Lily) and lost in the lake. Mia is not a character in the wardrobe; only Lily is. No outfit names the bracelet. No issue here (Mia has no outfit to check).
13. Appearance only — Lily / standard: "Long-sleeve blue cotton top with a round neckline, green knitted cardigan with a front opening and wooden-look round fastenings, brown corduroy trousers with an elastic waist, and sturdy brown rubber boots." Pure appearance. Lily / costumed: "Long-sleeve purple swim shirt (rash-guard) with a round neckline covering the whole torso from shoulders to waist, and a single flowing orange silk scarf tied at the waist as a mermaid tail that replaces the legs from the waist down, with a loose fan-shaped fin of fabric at the end." Pure appearance. Lily / nightwear: "Short-sleeve yellow cotton pyjama top with a round neckline, matching yellow cotton pyjama bottoms with an elastic waist, and bare feet." Includes "bare feet" which writes a slot as empty rather than omitting it. Also pure appearance otherwise. The slot issue is covered under check 4.
14. Props — The silk scarf in the costumed outfit is functioning as a garment (makeshift tail), but it is a scarf, which is a garment. However, the shell bracelet is not listed in any outfit (Mia not in wardrobe). No prop listed as a garment. The scarf is a garment, not a prop. No issue.

Summary of faults:
- Check 1: Costume recognisability — Lily's costumed outfit uses a scarf as a tail, not a proper mermaid tail garment.
- Check 2: Drawability — the scarf is described by how it is knotted rather than by what it is.
- Check 4: Slot conflict — nightwear writes "bare feet" as footwear instead of omitting the slot.
- Check 6: Completeness — the costumed outfit does not have one tail from the waist down replacing the legs; it has a scarf tied at the waist reading as a skirt.

All these point to the costumed outfit needing a proper mermaid tail garment and the nightwear needing the bare feet slot omitted.
